ST-EN-01.title: The Secret Garden Door
ST-EN-01.audience: Year 7 readers studying suspense and discovery in narrative fiction
ST-EN-01.purpose: Engage readers through suspense as Mary discovers a hidden door.
ST-EN-01.context: A literary extract about a secret garden doorway being uncovered.

student_display.plain_text: One of the nice little gusts of wind rushed down the walk, and it was a stronger one than the rest. It was strong enough to wave the branches of the trees, and it was more than strong enough to sway the trailing sprays of untrimmed ivy hanging from the wall. Mary had stepped close to the robin, and suddenly the gust of wind swung aside some loose ivy trails, and more suddenly still she jumped toward it and caught it in her hand. This she did because she had seen something under it—a round knob which had been covered by the leaves hanging over it. It was the knob of a door. It was the lock of the door which had been closed ten years and she put her hand in her pocket, drew out the key and found it fitted the keyhole. She put the key in and turned it. It took two hands to do it, but it did turn. And then she took a long breath and looked behind her up the long walk to see if anyone was coming. No one was coming. No one ever did come, and she held back the swinging curtain of ivy and pushed back the door which opened slowly—slowly.

ST-EN-03.title: Country of Contrasts
ST-EN-03.audience: Year 7 readers studying Australian landscape poetry
ST-EN-03.purpose: Represent the Australian outback as both dangerous and life-giving.
ST-EN-03.context: A poem and context note about drought, monsoon, and resilience in the outback.

student_display.plain_text:
Part A: The Poem ("Country of Contrasts")
The red earth sleeps in midday heat,
A silent, baking, ancient clay,
Where spinifex and salt-bush meet,
Under a sky of endless grey.
But when the heavy monsoons blow,
The cracked clay turns to rushing jade,
As wild, brown torrents overflow,
And desert life is newly made.

A land of whispers and of screams,
Of ghost-gums stark against the night,
Where dry creeks hide their sapphire dreams,
And eagles wheel in blinding light.
We love the hazard and the grace,
The sudden flood, the burning air—
For time can never quite erase
The dark, sweet wonder sleeping there.

Part B: Context Note
This poem, written in the ballad tradition, explores the dual nature of the Australian outback. Unlike European pastoral poetry that celebrates mild, predictable landscapes, Australian literature often wrestles with ecological volatility—the sudden transition between catastrophic drought and life-giving deluge. The ghost-gum and spinifex serve as symbols of resilience, adapting to survive in environments that alternate between 'burning air' and 'rushing jade.'

ST-EN-04.title: The Eagle and The Seagull
ST-EN-04.audience: Year 7 readers comparing poetic representations of birds
ST-EN-04.purpose: Compare how two poems represent power, movement, and freedom.
ST-EN-04.context: A classic poem and a paired original poem about birds and natural freedom.

student_display.plain_text:
Poem 1: The Eagle (Alfred, Lord Tennyson)
He clasps the crag with crooked hands;
Close to the sun in lonely lands,
Ring'd with the azure world, he stands.

The wrinkled sea beneath him crawls;
He watches from his mountain walls,
And like a thunderbolt he falls.

Poem 2: The Seagull (Original)
She drifts upon the salty breeze,
A scrap of white above the seas,
At home with storms and wild disease.

She skims the crest of frothing waves,
And laughs at what the ocean braves,
Then nests in dark, forgotten caves.

Context Note
Tennyson's classic nineteenth-century poem 'The Eagle' uses high-level imagery to depict a solitary, majestic predator ruling from a mountain peak. In contrast, the modern paired piece 'The Seagull' describes a bird integrated with the ocean's chaotic energy. While the eagle stands motionless before a dramatic drop, the seagull is defined by constant, light motion ('drifts', 'skims'), presenting a different aspect of natural freedom.

ST-EN-05.title: Solitude
ST-EN-05.purpose: Explain a reflective argument about the value of being alone.
ST-EN-05.context: A reflective prose extract about solitude, society, and independent thought.

student_display.plain_text: I find it wholesome to be alone the greater part of the time. To be in company, even with the best, is soon wearisome and dissipating. I love to be alone. I never found the companion that was so companionable as solitude. We are for the most part more lonely when we go abroad among men than when we stay in our chambers. A man thinking or working is always alone, let him be where he will. Solitude is not measured by the miles of space that intervene between a man and his fellows. The really diligent student in one of the crowded hives of Cambridge College is as solitary as a dervish in the desert. Society is commonly too cheap. We meet at very short intervals, not having had time to acquire any new value for each other.

ST-EN-06.title: The Green Invasion of Our West
ST-EN-06.audience: Queensland readers concerned about agriculture and government action
ST-EN-06.purpose: Persuade readers that prickly pear requires urgent scientific intervention.
ST-EN-06.context: A 1921 Queensland editorial about prickly pear as an agricultural threat.

student_display.plain_text:
Editorial: The Green Invasion of Our West
Published in the Queensland Gazette, October 1921

The alarming spread of the Prickly Pear (Opuntia) across our state has reached proportions that can only be described as a national disaster. What began as an ornamental garden plant has transformed into a relentless green tide, swallow-tailing across our most fertile agricultural districts. Vast tracts of productive land in the Darling Downs and Fitzroy basins have been rendered utterly impenetrable, locked away by dense wall-to-wall thickets of thorns.

The biology of this weed makes containment a nightmare. The plant propagates rapidly through vegetative segments carried by livestock, as well as seeds distributed by native birds. Currently, our struggling landholders are locked in an unequal struggle. They are forced to spend their life savings on mechanical clearing and highly toxic arsenic pentoxide, with little to show for their labour but ruined health and empty pockets.

The thickets are now so dense that they completely choke out native grasses, starving cattle and forcing families to abandon their homesteads. Agricultural settlement has ground to a halt. We must face the hard truth: manual and chemical clearing have failed. The government must urgently fund and investigate a biological solution, such as the importation of the Cactoblastis moth. Without scientific intervention, we risk losing the heart of our country to this silent invader.

ST-EN-07.title: The Thin Blue Line
ST-EN-07.audience: Museum visitors and Year 7 science-literacy readers
ST-EN-07.purpose: Inform visitors about the atmosphere's composition, layers, and protective role.
ST-EN-07.context: A museum exhibit panel explaining Earth's atmosphere and its layers.

student_display.plain_text:
Museum Exhibit Panel: The Thin Blue Line

Earth's atmosphere is a delicate, protective jacket of gases that wraps around our planet, insulating us from the freezing vacuum of space and providing the oxygen essential for life. This gaseous envelope is composed of approximately seventy-eight per cent nitrogen, twenty-one per cent oxygen, and trace amounts of other elements including argon, carbon dioxide, and water vapour.

To scientists, the atmosphere is not uniform; it is divided into five distinct layers defined by temperature fluctuations: the troposphere, the stratosphere, the mesosphere, the thermosphere, and the exosphere. The lowest layer, the troposphere, extends from the surface up to about twelve kilometres. It is here that almost all weather events and cloud formations occur. As altitude increases within the troposphere, air pressure and air density decrease rapidly. This creates significant challenges for high-altitude flight and respiratory function, as the air molecules grow sparser.

Above this, the stratosphere houses the crucial ozone layer, which filters out harmful ultraviolet radiation. By studying how these layers interact, meteorologists can forecast weather patterns and climate scientists can predict long-term global changes. From space, this entire life-support system appears as a thin, luminous blue band—a fragile shield protecting all terrestrial life.

ST-EN-09.title: Queensland Drought: Settler Letter and Climate Account
ST-EN-09.audience: Year 7 readers comparing historical and contemporary accounts
ST-EN-09.purpose: Compare personal experience of drought with a modern explanatory account.
ST-EN-09.context: A settler letter from 1896 paired with a recent climate history excerpt.

student_display.plain_text:
Text A (Letter from Edward Vance, Queensland settler, October 1896):
"The earth has split into deep fissures, and the waterhole is nothing but a caked floor of grey mud. We lost ten heifers this week; they simply collapsed under the heat. The sky is a brass bowl, reflecting a sun that is furious and relentless. We watch the horizon every afternoon, praying for a cloud, but only dust rises in the distance, whipped up by a scorching westerly wind that parches our throats."

Text B (Excerpt from 'Historical Climate Patterns of Queensland', 2024):
"The drought of 1896 represents one of the earliest recorded El Niño events in post-settlement Queensland. Meteorological reports indicate that rainfall fell below the tenth percentile for nine consecutive months. This led to severe soil moisture deficits, devastating agricultural yields and causing widespread livestock mortality. Unlike modern farmers, nineteenth-century settlers lacked access to subterranean bores or satellite forecasting, leaving them highly vulnerable to these severe climate fluctuations."

ST-EN-10.title: Sashiko Stitches
ST-EN-10.audience: Year 7 readers studying cultural memory in narrative writing
ST-EN-10.purpose: Show how a craft connects a young narrator to family and cultural history.
ST-EN-10.context: A narrative extract about learning Sashiko embroidery from a grandmother.

student_display.plain_text: My grandmother's hands are maps of a long journey, her knuckles bent like the roots of the old pine in our backyard. Every afternoon, she sits by the window, her needle diving in and out of the blue indigo cloth. She is teaching me Sashiko—a traditional Japanese embroidery technique that uses a simple running stitch to create geometric patterns. "This is not just for decoration," she whispers, her accent soft but firm. "Sashiko was born in the cold winters of northern Japan, where poor farming families stitched scraps of cloth together to make their thin clothes warmer and stronger." I look at the white cotton thread against the blue fabric, forming a pattern of overlapping waves. With each stitch, I am not just joining fabric; I am anchoring myself to a history I have only ever read about in schoolbooks.

Inside, the air was thick with the scent of grease, damp wool, and eucalyptus, a pungent perfume that defined life on the station. Young Thomas stood near the sorting table, his hands calloused despite his fourteen years, watching his father guide the clacking shears. The sheep lay docile in the older man's grip, its fleece falling away in a single, greasy cream blanket. Outside, the red dust of the western plains stretched toward a horizon that shimmered in the heat-haze, a vast and silent ocean of spinifex and clay pan. It was a harsh country, but Thomas knew no other home, and in the quiet efficiency of his father's movements, he felt a deep, unspoken security.

ST-EN-15.title: Our Suburbs Need Green Lungs
ST-EN-15.purpose: Persuade readers to protect urban green space from development.
ST-EN-15.context: A letter to the editor about proposed development of Oakwood Common.

student_display.plain_text:
Letter to the Editor: Our Suburbs Need Green Lungs
Published in the Metro Daily, March 2026

I write to express my deep concern over the proposed development of the Oakwood Common into a high-density apartment complex. In our haste to accommodate a growing population, we are systematically destroying the very spaces that make our suburbs liveable. The Oakwood Common is not merely a vacant block of land; it is a vital wildlife corridor, home to nesting kookaburras, possums, and a stand of century-old red gums.

Urban green spaces are the 'lungs' of our communities. Scientific research has consistently shown that access to nature reduces stress, encourages physical activity, and fosters a sense of community. By replacing grass with concrete, we are contributing to the 'urban heat island' effect and isolating our children from the natural world. Once these pockets of green are paved over, they are gone forever. We must demand that our local council protects Oakwood Common. Let us choose community health and ecological stewardship over short-term financial gain.

ST-EN-16.title: A Plastic-Free Canteen
ST-EN-16.audience: Year 7 assembly audience and school decision-makers
ST-EN-16.purpose: Persuade the school community to remove single-use plastic from the canteen.
ST-EN-16.context: A student council speech draft for a Year 7 assembly.

student_display.plain_text:
Speech Draft: A Plastic-Free Canteen
Delivered by Student Council Representative, Year 7 Assembly

Every day, our school canteen generates over five hundred pieces of single-use plastic wrapping, bottles, and utensils. Most of this waste ends up in our schoolyard or landfill, where it will take hundreds of years to break down. We pride ourselves on being a forward-thinking school, but our daily practices tell a different story. It is time for a change.

By transitioning to biodegradable packaging and encouraging students to bring reusable containers, we can eliminate plastic waste from our canteen entirely. Some argue that reusable items are inconvenient, but is convenience worth the cost of our environment? Our oceans are choking on plastic, and our local marine life is suffering. We have the power to make a difference, starting right here in our own courtyard. Let us lead by example and show that our school cares about the future of our planet.

ST-EN-17.title: Lights in the Deep
ST-EN-17.audience: Year 7 readers learning science vocabulary through information text
ST-EN-17.purpose: Explain bioluminescence and its survival functions in deep-sea organisms.
ST-EN-17.context: A science article about light-producing organisms in the midnight zone.

student_display.plain_text:
Science Article: Lights in the Deep

In the midnight zone of the ocean, where sunlight never penetrates and the pressure is crushing, creatures have evolved a remarkable ability: bioluminescence. This is the production and emission of light by a living organism, a chemical reaction that takes place inside specialized cells called photophores. Unlike artificial light bulbs, which release heat, bioluminescence is 'cold light,' meaning less than twenty per cent of the energy is lost as heat.

Deep-sea organisms use this living light for survival in three primary ways: hunting, defense, and communication. The anglerfish uses a glowing lure dangling above its mouth to attract curious prey. Other species, like the hatchetfish, use bioluminescence on their undersides to match the faint light filtering from above, a camouflage technique known as counterillumination. In a dark, vast wilderness, these glowing signals serve as lanterns of survival, showing that even in the deepest shadow, life finds a way to shine.

ST-EN-19.title: Ballarat Goldfields: Journal and Historical Account
ST-EN-19.audience: Year 7 readers comparing personal and historical accounts
ST-EN-19.purpose: Compare a miner's experience with a broader historical explanation of the gold rush.
ST-EN-19.context: A goldfields journal entry paired with a recent historical account.

student_display.plain_text:
Text A (Journal Entry of William Barlow, Ballarat Goldfields, October 1852):
'We have been digging for three weeks now in the yellow clay, our backs aching and our hands blistered. The tent is damp, and the water in the creek is thick with mud. Yet, when we wash the cradle and see those tiny, glittering grains of gold catching the light, all the fatigue vanishes. We live on mutton and damper, and the noise of the wind through the tents at night is a lonely sound, but the hope of a rich strike keeps us all chained to the earth.'

Text B (Excerpt from 'The Golden Shapers of Australia', 2023):
'The Australian gold rushes of the 1850s triggered a massive wave of global migration, doubling the country's population in a single decade. This rapid influx of people transformed Australia from a remote penal colony into a wealthy, diverse society. The goldfields became crucible sites for democratic ideas, leading to events like the Eureka Stockade. However, the environmental cost was severe, as creeks were diverted, hillsides cleared, and massive amounts of sediment washed into local river systems.'

ST-EN-20.context: A narrative extract about learning to knead bread with a grandfather.

student_display.plain_text: My grandfather's kitchen is a sanctuary of warm air and white dust, the air smelling of yeast and sweet flour. On the wooden table, a mound of dough rests under a clean tea towel, rising slowly in the morning sun. He teaches me the art of kneading—pushing the dough away with the heel of my hand, folding it over, and turning it. 'It requires patience,' he says, his voice steady and calm. 'You cannot rush the yeast.' As my hands work the dough, feeling it transform from a sticky mass into a smooth, elastic ball, I feel a quiet link to my ancestors who baked bread in outdoor stone ovens. In a world of instant messages and fast food, this slow, tactile rhythm is a grounding anchor, connecting my modern life to a timeless human tradition.

ST-EN-21.title: Arrival at Sydney Cove
ST-EN-21.audience: Year 7 readers analysing perspective and setting
ST-EN-21.purpose: Represent a new arrival's mixed fear and hope in an unfamiliar landscape.
ST-EN-21.context: A historical narrative extract set at Sydney Cove in 1790.

student_display.plain_text: The wooden hull of the transport ship creaked groaningly as it finally anchored in the sheltered waters of Sydney Cove. Standing on the damp deck, young James pulled his threadbare woollen coat tighter against the brisk morning air of October 1790. Before him lay a landscape that felt entirely alien. Instead of the soft, green, rolling meadows of his home in Somerset, the hillsides here were crowded with strange, dark-foliaged trees that shed their bark in long, ragged strips rather than their leaves. The air was filled not with the familiar songs of thrushes, but with the harsh, screeching cries of cockatoos that wheeled overhead like white fragments of cloud. Yet, as the morning sun broke through the grey haze, it cast a brilliant, golden warmth over the sandstone cliffs, gilding the ripples of the harbour. In that sudden light, the wilderness seemed less like a prison and more like a vast, unwritten page.

The temperature plunged instantly, and the air smelled of wet stone, earth, and ancient moss. Overhead, the ceiling was crowded with delicate, straw-like stalactites, from which drops of water fell with a rhythmic, metallic ring into the pools below. Our guide shone her torch toward the far wall, where the dark rock was covered in a soft, emerald-green glow. It was a colony of glow-worms, their tiny bioluminescent threads hanging down like a curtain of living stardust. Looking at those quiet, pulsing lights in the deep silence of the earth, I felt as though we had stumbled into a hidden cathedral, a secret sanctuary where time had stood still for ten thousand years.

ST-EN-23.title: The Fire-Bringer
ST-EN-23.audience: Year 7 readers studying metaphor and ecological theme
ST-EN-23.purpose: Represent bushfire as destructive and regenerative.
ST-EN-23.context: A poem and context note about fire in the Australian landscape.

student_display.plain_text:
Part A: The Poem ("The Fire-Bringer")
The summer wind is hot and dry,
A searing breath across the plain,
Under a white and copper sky,
That holds no promise of the rain.
And then the spark, a sudden flash,
The red beast leaps from branch to bough,
It turns the forest floor to ash,
And crowns the hills with crimson brow.

It roars and sweeps with hungry jaws,
A wall of orange, fierce and bright,
Ignoring all of nature's laws,
To turn the midday into night.
Yet when the blackened ruins sleep,
The green shoots burst from charred wood,
As life and beauty slowly creep,
To show the fire's work was good.

Part B: Context Note
This poem explores the dual nature of bushfires in the Australian landscape. Using the metaphor of a 'red beast' with 'hungry jaws,' the poet personifies the destructive force of the fire. However, the final stanza shifts to a theme of regeneration, highlighting how many native plants require the intense heat of fire to release seeds and stimulate new growth, framing fire as an agent of ecological rebirth.

ST-EN-24.title: Central Station and Forest Dawn
ST-EN-24.audience: Year 7 readers comparing sensory language in paired poems
ST-EN-24.purpose: Contrast urban bustle with natural stillness.
ST-EN-24.context: Paired poems about a city station and a forest morning.

student_display.plain_text:
Poem 1: Central Station at 5 PM (Original)
A torrent of faces, hurried and grey,
Streams through the gates at the end of the day,
The clacking of heels on the concrete floor,
The mechanical hum of the sliding door.
Beneath the cold glare of the station light,
We rush to our trains and escape to the night.

Poem 2: The Forest Dawn (Original)
A whisper of breeze in the canopy high,
Where pale eucalypts touch the soft morning sky,
The warble of magpies, a clear, golden note,
That drifts on the mist from a feathery throat.
The green leaves are drinking the first wash of sun,
As a quiet, new day has in silence begun.

Context Note
These paired poems contrast the sensory experiences of urban bustle and natural stillness. 'Central Station' uses regular, driving rhythm and auditory imagery ('clacking', 'mechanical hum') to convey the hurried, repetitive nature of modern city life. In contrast, 'The Forest Dawn' uses soft alliteration ('whisper of breeze', 'soft morning sky') and a slower pace to evoke a sense of peace and natural harmony.

ST-EN-25.title: Let the Wild Brumbies Run
ST-EN-25.audience: Readers debating environmental and cultural heritage issues
ST-EN-25.purpose: Persuade readers to oppose culling wild horses in Kosciuszko National Park.
ST-EN-25.context: A letter to the editor about wild brumby management.

student_display.plain_text:
Letter to the Editor: Let the Wild Brumbies Run
Published in the Alpine Herald, April 2026

I write to express my strong opposition to the proposed cull of wild horses (brumbies) in the Kosciuszko National Park. These magnificent animals are not merely pests to be eradicated; they are a living part of our heritage, immortalized in the poetry of Banjo Paterson and woven into the cultural identity of the high country. To shoot them from helicopters is a cruel and unnecessary practice that outrages many Australians.

While environmentalists argue that the horses damage fragile alpine wetlands and native vegetation, we must consider more humane management strategies, such as rehoming or fertility control. The brumbies have roamed these mountains for over a century, adapting to the harsh climate and becoming a symbol of wild freedom. Surely, in a country as vast as ours, we can find a way to balance ecological conservation with the preservation of our cultural history, rather than resorting to mass slaughter.

ST-EN-27.title: The Wood Wide Web
ST-EN-27.audience: Year 7 readers learning ecology through information text
ST-EN-27.purpose: Explain how forest trees share resources and warnings through fungal networks.
ST-EN-27.context: A science article about mycorrhizal networks in native eucalypt forests.

student_display.plain_text:
Science Article: The Wood Wide Web

In a native eucalypt forest, the trees are not isolated individuals competing for sunlight; they are members of a complex, interconnected community. Beneath the soil, a vast network of fungal threads, known as mycorrhizae, links the roots of different trees together. This underground system, often referred to by scientists as the 'wood wide web,' allows trees to share resources and communicate with one another.

Through these fungal connections, a mature 'mother tree' can transport sugars, nitrogen, and phosphorus to younger seedlings struggling in the shade. Furthermore, if a tree is attacked by insects, it can send chemical warning signals through the network, prompting neighbouring trees to increase their chemical defences. This symbiotic relationship between fungi and trees shows that cooperation, rather than competition, is a fundamental driver of forest ecosystems.

ST-EN-29.title: Overland Telegraph: Operator Letter and Historical Account
ST-EN-29.audience: Year 7 readers comparing firsthand and historical accounts
ST-EN-29.purpose: Compare a telegraph operator's excitement with a broader historical explanation.
ST-EN-29.context: A telegraph operator's 1872 letter paired with a recent historical account.

student_display.plain_text:
Text A (Letter from Clara Higgins, Telegraph Operator, Alice Springs, October 1872):
"The line is finally joined, and the first message has flashed through to Adelaide! It is hard to believe that our lonely station is now linked to the rest of the world. We sit in our small stone building, listening to the constant, rhythmic clicking of the key. Outside, the red sand stretches forever, and the heat is a heavy weight, but when the key begins to tap, we feel a sudden rush of connection, as if the vast distance of the interior has vanished in an instant."

Text B (Excerpt from 'The Wire that Bound Australia', 2024):
"The completion of the Overland Telegraph Line in 1872 was a milestone in Australian history, reducing communication times between Australia and London from months to a few hours. The project required the erection of over thirty thousand wooden poles across the arid interior, a massive engineering feat. While it integrated the colonies into the global economy, it also disrupted Indigenous communities along the route, bringing new settlements and ecological pressures to fragile desert environments."

ST-EN-30.title: Pandanus Weaving
ST-EN-30.audience: Year 7 readers studying cultural heritage and sensory detail
ST-EN-30.purpose: Show how weaving links a young narrator to cultural heritage and family teaching.
ST-EN-30.context: A narrative extract about learning pandanus weaving from a grandmother.

student_display.plain_text: My grandmother's back porch is a sanctuary of dry grass and warm wood, smelling of sun-baked reeds and tea. In her lap, a bundle of long, green pandanus leaves rests in a tub of water, softening in the heat. She is teaching me the art of weaving—how to split the leaf with a thumbnail, loop it over, and pull it taut. 'It takes time to learn the rhythm,' she says, her hands moving with a swift, instinctive grace. 'If you pull too hard, the leaf will split; if you are too loose, the basket will lose its shape.' As my fingers work the grass, feeling the rough fibers smooth out, I feel a quiet link to the generations of weavers who gathered by the same creeks. In a world of flashing screens, this slow, tactile craft is a grounding anchor, binding my modern life to a timeless cultural heritage.

student_display.plain_text:
FROM TAKE–MAKE–WASTE TO A CIRCULAR ECONOMY

A linear system extracts materials, makes products and discards them after use. A circular system aims to keep products and materials in use for longer.

REDESIGN: make products easier to repair, refill or disassemble.
REUSE: use an item again without turning it into a new material.
RECOVERY: collect useful materials or energy that would otherwise be lost.
STEWARDSHIP: assign responsibility for a product across more of its life cycle.

Example: a refillable container may reduce the need to manufacture and discard single-use packaging.

DESIGN AND PRODUCTION
Products may be designed for a short use even when the material lasts for decades.

USE AND DISPOSAL
Litter, poorly contained waste and lost equipment can enter drains, rivers and coastal waters.

TRANSPORT
Wind, rain, currents and floods can move plastic far from where it was discarded.

ECOLOGICAL EFFECTS
Animals may become entangled in larger items or ingest smaller fragments. Plastics can also carry organisms and chemicals.

Possible interventions include product redesign, collection systems, litter prevention, clean-up and enforcement.

ST-EN-Y7-P0-01.title: Screen Time: Limit or Lifeline?
ST-EN-Y7-P0-01.audience: Year 7 readers analysing a balanced opinion column about technology use at school and home
ST-EN-Y7-P0-01.purpose: Present two sides of a screen-time debate and propose a compromise for students.
ST-EN-Y7-P0-01.context: Original classroom opinion column written for Year 7 comprehension and evaluative-language practice.

student_display.plain_text:
Opinion column: Screen Time: Limit or Lifeline?

Adults often talk about students' screens as if every glowing rectangle is a trap. Critics warn that too much recreational screen time can shrink attention spans, increase distraction and make cyberbullying harder to escape. Some even claim that screens will 'rot our brains', a phrase that sounds dramatic because it turns a habit into a kind of damage.

Supporters see the issue differently. They argue that digital literacy is vital for future study and jobs: students need to search carefully, judge sources, design presentations and communicate online. A total ban would ignore the fact that technology is already part of modern learning.

The sensible solution is not panic or unlimited use. Schools and families should set a two-hour daily limit on recreational screen time during school days, while still allowing purposeful learning tasks. That boundary gives students time to read, talk face to face and rest their attention, without pretending that the digital world can simply be switched off.

ST-EN-Y7-P1-01.title: Caring for Willowbank Creek
ST-EN-Y7-P1-01.audience: Year 7 readers analysing respectful community information about Country, local place and consultation

student_display.plain_text:
Information article: Caring for Willowbank Creek

Willowbank Creek is easy to miss from the road. It slips behind the oval, bends past the paperbark trees and disappears under a concrete bridge near the bus stop. For many years, students treated it like a boundary: the place where the school ended. This term, the creek is being studied as a living part of the community.

The restoration project began after the local council, the school environment group and representatives from a nearby First Nations community met to discuss the creek's history and future. The project notes explain that the creek should not be described only as a 'drain' or a 'problem area'. It is habitat for frogs, insects and waterbirds; it also sits within Country that has been cared for and known across generations.

Students will test water clarity, record rubbish hotspots and design signs that ask visitors to stay on the path. Before any sign is installed, the wording will be checked with community representatives so that it avoids token language and does not pretend to speak for Elders. The signs will use precise, respectful phrases such as 'care for this place' and 'learn before you act', rather than slogans that sound powerful but explain nothing.

The project asks students to change how they see a familiar place. A creek beside a school is not just background scenery. It can be a text: its names, maps, warnings, plant lists and stories all shape how people understand responsibility.

The council is seeking community feedback on a raised timber walkway through the edge of Moreton Bay mangroves. The design would keep visitors above the mudflats, protect seedling areas with railings and include three viewing platforms with signs explaining tides, fish nurseries and shorebird habitat. Construction would occur outside the main bird-nesting season. The council says the project will improve access while reducing informal tracks that currently damage young mangroves.

If the walkway is built, the signs should not just say 'look at nature'. They should ask visitors to slow down, notice small life and leave without making the place feel like a theme park.

ST-EN-Y7-P1-03.title: The Closing Bell
ST-EN-Y7-P1-03.audience: Year 7 readers practising close analysis of character, setting, symbolism and theme

student_display.plain_text:
Literary extract: The Closing Bell

The last bell did not ring so much as shatter. It broke across the courtyard and sent everyone rushing: bags swinging, shoes slapping concrete, voices climbing over one another. Mira stayed still beside the noticeboard, staring at the folded blue paper half-hidden under the science-room door.

It was not hers. She knew that before she picked it up. The handwriting was Theo's, all sharp corners and impatient loops. At the top, in red pen, someone had written: Final warning. Beneath it was a note about missed homework, a parent meeting and the robotics competition he had been boasting about all week.

Mira heard Theo laughing near the lockers. He sounded exactly as he had at lunch when he told everyone that her bridge design would 'fold like wet cardboard'. Her face warmed at the memory. The paper felt thin in her hand, almost weightless, but the choice inside it was not.

She could leave it where it had fallen. She could wave it in the air and let his friends read every red sentence. Instead, Mira folded the warning along its old crease and slid it into the side pocket of his backpack as she passed. Theo did not notice.

At the gate, the wind lifted a scatter of jacaranda petals and pushed them against the fence. Mira watched the purple shapes gather, separate and gather again. Tomorrow, Theo might still laugh. Her bridge might still fail. But for one quiet moment, she had refused to become the kind of person he expected her to be.

Poem: Land Remembers

Red dust settles on cracked skin of earth. Old man sits by fire, smoke curling like ghost-spirit into night. He speaks of time before fences, when stars were maps and rivers were veins of life. We listen, silent, as words weave stories into soil. He says, 'Land is not thing to own, but mother who holds us.' His voice, gravel and honey, carries weight of ancestors. We watch firelight dance on his face, lines etched deep like dry creek beds. He tells of sacred places, hidden from eyes that only see profit. 'Respect Country,' he whispers, 'or lose your soul.' We feel pulse of earth beneath bare feet. It is heartbeat, steady and strong. We are small, but we are part of something vast. No money, not even $1,000,000, can buy this connection. It is gift, passed down through breath and blood. We learn to listen to wind, to read signs in flight of eagle. We are keepers of story now. We carry flame forward, honouring those who walked before. Land remembers. We remember.

ST-EN-Y7-P0-03.title: Old Jack of the Outback
ST-EN-Y7-P0-03.audience: Year 7 readers analysing ballad style, character and symbolism
ST-EN-Y7-P0-03.purpose: Provide a self-contained poem for analysing rhyme, rhythm, vernacular language, Australian bush setting and layers of meaning.
ST-EN-Y7-P0-03.context: Original classroom poem in a bush-ballad style for literary analysis.

student_display.plain_text:
Poem: Old Jack of the Outback

Out in the Outback, where the red dust flies,
Lived a grizzled prospector 'neath the burning skies.
Old Jack was his name, though none knew his age—
His life was the bush, and the land was his stage.

One morning he wandered through spinifex and stone,
Through country so harsh and so vast and so lone.
With his hammer and pick and his worn canvas pack,
He searched for the gold that would bring fortune back.

'I'll find me a fortune,' old Jack used to say,
'And I'll stake me a claim that'll brighten my day!'
But the years rolled along, and no fortune appeared,
Till one sweltering afternoon, something was cleared.

A glint in the rock made his weathered heart race,
Pure gold was exposed in that lonesome place.
With tears in his eyes and a cheer to the sky,
He hammered and dug, though his muscles were dry.

The nugget came free—it was worth near $500!
Jack danced in the desert beneath the red sky's hue.
He'd prospected for forty long, gruelling years,
And now all that hardship dissolved into tears.

But Jack was a man of the land, tried and true,
So he stayed in the Outback—there's nothing else new.
He built him a homestead of corrugated tin,
And he watched the red sunset paint gold from within.
